prompt: On the first cluster, `deny-all` was created without error and `stranger` still reached the shop. Why?

choices.text: The policy had a syntax error
choices.why: The API server checked it and accepted it.

choices.text: Policies only apply to new pods
choices.why: Calico applied the same file to running pods at once.

choices.text: Nothing enforced it
choices.why: Right. The network plugin enforces policies; kindnet's engine failed on this kernel, and the API server only stores them.

choices.text: `stranger` was in the same namespace
choices.why: It was in `other`.

prompt: After `deny-all` on the Calico cluster, why did `front`, in the same namespace as the shop, time out too?

choices.text: Its empty selector also picks `front`
choices.why: Right. It selects every pod in `shop` and allows nothing in; a namespace gives its own pods no exception.

choices.text: Calico blocks every connection by default
choices.why: Before the policy, `stranger` got an answer.

choices.text: `front` had no label for a rule to match
choices.why: It had `app=front`, and no rule allowed it yet.

choices.text: The DNS lookup of `shop` was blocked
choices.why: DNS failures say `bad address`; this was a timeout.

prompt: `allow-front` names port 8080, while the shop's Service listens on 80. Why 8080?
hint: Which packet does the policy see?

choices.text: Port 80 needs root inside the container
choices.why: That is about the container, not the policy.

choices.text: The pod receives it on 8080
choices.why: Right. The policy is checked at the pod, after the Service has translated 80 into 8080.

choices.text: Policies cannot name port 80 at all
choices.why: Any port can be named.

choices.text: 8080 covers both ports
choices.why: A port rule names exactly one port.

prompt: A namespace has `deny-all` and `allow-front`. Someone adds a third policy that allows the shop from everywhere. What happens to `deny-all`?
hint: Can one policy take away what another grants?

choices.text: It wins, because it was applied first
choices.why: Order plays no part.

choices.text: The API server refuses the new policy as a conflict
choices.why: There are no conflicts; permissions add up.

choices.text: Both are ignored
choices.why: Each still selects pods; the allows simply add up.

choices.text: It still applies, and the shop opens up
choices.why: Right. It still selects the pods, and a connection is allowed if any policy allows it.

prompt: Why is selecting a namespace by `purpose: monitoring` riskier than by `kubernetes.io/metadata.name`?

choices.text: Custom labels are ignored by Calico
choices.why: Calico honoured it the moment it was added.

choices.text: Anyone who may label it can open it
choices.why: Right. The name label is set by Kubernetes and cannot be changed.

choices.text: It is slower to evaluate
choices.why: Speed is not the issue.

choices.text: It matches pods instead of namespaces
choices.why: It is a `namespaceSelector`.

prompt: After `front-egress`, `wget shop` from `front` failed with `bad address 'shop'`. What was blocked?

choices.text: The shop's port 8080 itself
choices.why: That was allowed by `front-egress`.

choices.text: The DNS query to CoreDNS
choices.why: Right. Port 53 to `kube-system` was not allowed out.

choices.text: The Service's ClusterIP
choices.why: No address was ever looked up, so none was blocked.

choices.text: Ingress into `front`
choices.why: Nothing restricts traffic into `front`.

prompt: In `front-dns`, the `namespaceSelector` and the `podSelector` sit in one `to` entry. What would two separate entries, each with its own dash, allow?
hint: Inside one entry they combine; across entries they add.

choices.text: The same thing
choices.why: Separate entries are alternatives, not one combined rule.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: Each entry would allow something on its own.

choices.text: Any `kube-dns` pod anywhere, or any pod in `kube-system`
choices.why: Right. Two entries are an OR, and far wider.

choices.text: Only pods in `shop`
choices.why: Neither entry mentions `shop`.

prompt: Put in order the steps that locked `front` down to the shop and DNS while keeping it working.
items: Install a plugin that enforces policies
trap: Without a plugin that enforces them, every later step changes nothing; and the DNS rule is only needed once egress is restricted.

prompt: A policy with `podSelector: {}` selects ___ pod in its namespace.
hint: An empty selector matches without conditions.
